payload.prompt: What is the spotter telling him?

audio.description: A synthesized calm voice says: clear high, clear high, stay there.

options.text: You can move up the track.
A wreck is ahead.
Pit this lap.

explanation.correct: Clear high means there is nothing on your high side, so you can move up the track.
explanation.incorrect: Clear high says the high side is open. A wreck or a pit call would sound different and more urgent.

payload.prompt: What is this call?

audio.description: A synthesized voice says: three wide below, three wide below, hold your line.

options.text: Three cars alongside.
Wreck ahead.
Pit road is closed.

explanation.correct: Three wide means three cars side by side, so hold your line and give everyone room.
explanation.incorrect: Three wide means three cars across the track. A wreck call uses the word wreck, and pit road news comes from the crew chief.
explanation.sayThisLine: He is three wide down there.

payload.prompt: What should he do?

audio.description: A synthesized urgent voice says: wreck ahead, wreck ahead, stay high, stay high.

options.text: Stay high.
Go low.
Stop on the track.

explanation.correct: Wreck ahead, stay high means the danger is low and the open lane is high.
explanation.incorrect: The spotter told him to stay high to miss the wreck. Stopping on track or ducking low would put him right in it.
explanation.sayThisLine: The spotter saved him from the wreck.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: The spotter said he was clear and he moved up and got hit.

options.text: Either the spotter missed a car or the call was late; spotters are human.
Spotters never make mistakes.
Drivers ignore their spotters.

payload.translation: Spotters work hard but can miss a car or call it a moment late.

followUps.line: It is a split-second job at 180 mph, so a miss can happen.
followUps.why: It shows you understand the pressure without blaming anyone.

followUps.line: The driver has to hear it and act immediately too.
followUps.why: Two people both have to get it right for a call to work.

payload.prompt: What is the spotter's primary job?

options.text: To watch the pit crew and verify tires.
To watch from high above the track and call out nearby cars and open lanes.
To track fuel and tell the driver when to pit.

explanation.correct: Right. The spotter sits high above the track with a radio and calls where every nearby car is. It is a second set of eyes for a driver with big blind spots.
explanation.incorrect: Pit strategy and fuel belong to the crew chief, and the pit crew handles tires. The spotter's job is to see what the driver cannot and say it fast.

payload.prompt: Does the spotter decide when the car pits?

scene.alt: A driver in the car with a spotter high above the track.

choices.label: No, the crew chief makes the pit call.
Yes, the spotter calls pit stops.

explanation.correct: Right. The crew chief makes pit and strategy calls; the spotter watches traffic and tells the driver where the other cars are.
explanation.incorrect: The spotter is the eyes, not the brain. Pit timing is the crew chief's call, made from the pit box.

payload.prompt: "Car left" means a car is {{meaning}}.

options: about to pit on the left
a mile behind on the left

explanation.correct: Yes. Car left warns that someone is right beside you on the left, so do not move that way.
explanation.incorrect: Car left is a warning about a car alongside on the left. It is about traffic right now, not pit plans or cars far behind.

lessons.title: Reading the loop data
lessons.objective: Read laps led and average running position.

payload.prompt: What does loop data tell you?

options.text: Only finishing position.
Average running position and speed, which show who was really fast.
How many pit stops a driver made.

explanation.correct: Right. Loop data tracks things like a driver's average running position and fastest laps, so you can see how strong the car was all race.
explanation.incorrect: Finishing position is on the results sheet already. Loop data adds running position and speed across the whole race, which can tell a different story from the finish.

payload.prompt: Led 180 of 400 laps. How many laps did others lead?

explanation.correct: Right. 400 minus 180 equals 220. Leading a lot of laps shows a strong car, but it does not guarantee the win.
explanation.incorrect: If one driver led 180 of 400 laps, everyone else combined led 220. Laps led measures time in front, not the final result.

payload.prompt: Laps led counts the laps a driver spent {{where}}.
payload.template: Laps led counts the laps a driver spent {{where}}.

explanation.correct: Yes. A lap is led when the car is first on the track at the line. Many laps led usually means a fast car.
explanation.incorrect: Laps led counts only time in first place, not time in the top ten or on the lead lap.

payload.prompt: Led 250 laps, best loop data, finished second. What is a fair read?

options.text: The car was probably fastest, but strategy, a caution or a late pass can still decide a race.
The loop data must be wrong, because the fastest car always wins.
Laps led only count at short tracks.

explanation.correct: Right. Laps led and loop data show a dominant car, and a caution, pit call or late pass can still cost the win.
explanation.incorrect: Laps led count everywhere, and the fastest car does not always win. That gap between speed and result is exactly what loop data helps you see.

payload.prompt: Whose numbers show the stronger car over the whole race?

options.label: Driver A; the data shows a dominant car.
options.consequence: That is what the stats say. Driver B won, probably through late strategy or track position, but A was stronger across the race.

options.label: Driver B; winning proves it.
options.consequence: B earned the win, but the numbers measure the whole race, and they point to A.
considerations: Twenty laps led is very few.
The win came at the end.

payload.expertNote: Speed and victory are not the same thing. Fans who read loop data see the fuller picture, and can say both 'he earned the win' and 'the other car was faster'.

lessons.title: Dominant but did not win
lessons.objective: Explain why the fastest car does not always win.

payload.prompt: The fastest car finished fifth after a late caution. Fair read?

options.label: Speed and results differ; the caution reshuffled the order.
options.consequence: The stats back it up. He was dominant, and a late caution handed his rivals track position. That is racing.

options.label: The driver must have made a mistake.
options.consequence: Nothing in the facts says so. A fast car can lose position on a caution without anyone doing anything wrong.

payload.expertNote: The fastest car does not always win. Strategy and luck matter, and fans who understand this are kinder and sharper in a conversation.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: He led the whole race and got second. How?

options.text: A caution or pit strategy can cost even the fastest car the win.
Leading all race means he must have won.
Laps led are not counted in the final result.

payload.translation: Leading and having the fastest car is not the same as winning.

followUps.line: A caution or pit call can shuffle everything. Speed is one force; strategy and luck are others.
followUps.why: It explains that races are decided by more than speed.

followUps.line: That must have been painful to watch.
followUps.why: Sympathy first, analysis second, is the friendliest order.

payload.prompt: Does the fastest car always win?

scene.alt: A lap chart showing a fast car that led early but faded late.

explanation.correct: Right. Speed is one force among several. Cautions, pit strategy and track position reshuffle races all the time.
explanation.incorrect: The fastest car does not always win. Cautions, pit calls and track position shift races, so speed is necessary but not enough.

payload.prompt: What often matters more than raw speed late in a race?

options.text: The driver's experience level.
Track position, because it is hard to pass.
The size of the pit crew.

explanation.correct: Right. On tracks where passing is hard, a car in front can often hold off a faster car behind, which is why pit strategy chases track position.
explanation.incorrect: Every team has the same size of crew, and experience helps but does not beat position. Late in a race, where you are running often matters more than how fast you could go.

payload.prompt: A late {{event}} can erase a long lead by bunching the field.
payload.template: A late {{event}} can erase a long lead by bunching the field.

explanation.correct: Yes. A caution packs the field back up behind the pace car, so a big lead disappears in one lap.
explanation.incorrect: Only a caution bunches the field. A green-flag run stretches it out, and qualifying happens before the race.

payload.prompt: Does a damaged car get unlimited repair time?

scene.alt: A damaged car being worked on in the garage.

choices.label: No, there is a time limit.

explanation.correct: Right. The damaged vehicle policy puts the repair on a clock. Beat it and the car can rejoin; miss it and the car is done for the day.
explanation.incorrect: The damaged vehicle policy limits repair time. If the clock runs out before the car is ready, it is out of the race.

payload.prompt: Why does NASCAR have a damaged vehicle time limit?

options.text: To keep the race moving and stop long repairs from dragging on.
To punish teams for crashing.
To keep wrecker trucks busy.

explanation.correct: Right. The clock forces a decision: fix it quickly and get back out, or end the day. It is about race flow, not punishment.
explanation.incorrect: Crashing already costs a team plenty, so the limit is not a punishment. It exists so repairs cannot drag on and the race keeps moving.

payload.prompt: If the repair clock runs out, the team {{result}}.
payload.template: If the repair clock runs out, the team {{result}}.

explanation.correct: Right. When the clock hits zero the car is done for the day. No special restart and no second chance.
explanation.incorrect: Running out of time is final: the team is out of the race. It does not get a fresh start or a free tire change.

payload.prompt: The repair needs more time than the clock allows. What do you do?

facts.label: Damage
facts.value: Fixable, but it takes longer than the clock allows

facts.label: Clock
facts.value: Short of what the repair needs

facts.label: Rule
facts.value: Miss the clock and the car is out

options.label: Accept that the day is over and save the car.
options.consequence: The clock is the rule. A rushed fix that fails on track is risky and gains nothing once the time has run out.

options.label: Rush a partial fix and hope to beat the clock.
options.consequence: It is a gamble. If the partial fix works in time the car rejoins, but a bad fix can be unsafe or slow.

payload.expertNote: The exact time limit has changed over the years, so check the current rulebook. The idea stays the same: repair fast or be done.

payload.prompt: What are common NASCAR penalties?

options.text: Points loss, crew chief suspension and fines.
Only fines, never suspensions.
Automatic disqualification for any violation.

explanation.correct: Right. NASCAR can take away points, suspend a crew chief or other crew members, issue fines and penalize positions. Bigger violations get bigger penalties.
explanation.incorrect: Penalties scale with the violation: fines and points are common, suspensions happen for bigger infractions, and disqualification is reserved for the most serious ones.

payload.prompt: Can a car be disqualified after the race for failing inspection?

scene.alt: Tech inspectors checking a race car.

choices.label: Yes, if it fails post-race inspection.
No, results are final at the flag.

explanation.correct: Yes. Post-race inspection can overturn a result if a car is found illegal. It is rare, but it is why fans say a win is not official until the car passes the tech line.
explanation.incorrect: Results are not always final at the flag. A car that fails post-race inspection can lose its finish. It is rare, but possible.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: His crew chief got suspended. That's brutal.

options.text: It hurts because the crew chief calls the strategy and adjustments.
Crew chiefs do not matter much to results.
Suspensions are never given.

payload.translation: Losing the crew chief for a race is a real blow because strategy is often as important as speed.

followUps.line: The crew chief makes the pit calls and adjustments, so losing them for a race hurts.
followUps.why: It shows you know what the role does, not just the name.

followUps.line: Who is calling the race in their place?
followUps.why: A curious question keeps the chat friendly and invites her knowledge.

payload.prompt: A suspended crew chief cannot {{role}} that weekend.
payload.template: A suspended crew chief cannot {{role}} that weekend.

options: call strategy from the pit box
gaps.correct: call strategy from the pit box

explanation.correct: Yes. The crew chief's main job is strategy and adjustments, and a suspension takes that seat away for the weekend.
explanation.incorrect: Crew chiefs neither drive nor change tires. Their role is strategy from the pit box, which is what a suspension removes.

payload.prompt: What does NASCAR inspection focus on?

options.text: Only engine and fuel.
The whole car: body, weight, aero parts, engine and fuel.
Safety gear only.

explanation.correct: Right. Inspectors check the body shape, weight, aero parts, engine and fuel, because small differences can add up to speed.
explanation.incorrect: Inspection covers the whole car, not one system. Body shape, weight, aero parts, engine and fuel are all checked, along with safety equipment.

lessons.title: Reading a race from the lap chart
lessons.objective: Read a race from its chart.

payload.prompt: Put these race events in order.

items.text: Lap 1: race begins in qualifying order.
Lap 60: stage break, first pit cycle.
Lap 62: order shuffles; pit winners lead.
Lap 120: stage break, second pit cycle.

explanation.correct: Right. A lap chart shows the running order changing lap by lap, and pit cycles are the moments the field reshuffles.
explanation.incorrect: The order is start, first stage break and pit cycle, reshuffle, green-flag racing, second stage break and pit cycle, reshuffle. Pit cycles are the reset buttons on a lap chart.

payload.prompt: What can a lap chart show you?

options.text: Exact pit stop times and fuel savings.
Who ran where each lap, who gained on pit road and when cautions fell.
Only final positions.

explanation.correct: Right. A lap chart is the race as a story: who led when, who moved up, who faded, and when the order got shuffled.
explanation.incorrect: A lap chart tracks running position lap by lap. It does not give stop times or fuel figures, and it shows far more than the final order.

payload.prompt: On a lap chart, who won the pit cycle?

options.text: The car that left pit road first or gained the most places.
The car with the youngest crew chief.
The car that pitted earliest in the day.

explanation.correct: Right. A pit-cycle winner comes out of the stops ahead of where it went in, so the lap chart shows the car climbing.
explanation.incorrect: Age of the crew chief and the time of the first stop do not matter. You win the pit cycle by leaving pit road ahead of the cars you were racing.

payload.prompt: A lap chart tracks {{what}} and shows {{reveals}}.
payload.template: A lap chart tracks {{what}} and shows {{reveals}}.

explanation.correct: Yes. A lap chart is a position story, and pit cycles are when the field reshapes.
explanation.incorrect: A lap chart records where each car ran at each lap. That lets you see who won the pit battles, not the paint or the driver's age.

payload.prompt: Driver A led. After the pit cycle, Driver B leads. What does the chart say?

facts.label: Pit stops
facts.value: B took two tires; A took four

options.label: B gained track position with a shorter stop.
options.consequence: That is the read. Two tires is quicker, so B left pit road ahead and took the lead.
considerations: Two tires is a faster stop.

options.label: A must have made a mistake.
options.consequence: Nothing in the chart says so. Read the position shift and the stops before assigning blame.
considerations: The chart shows a position swap.

payload.expertNote: Pit cycles are where many races are decided, and a lap chart shows exactly who gained on pit road.
